phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar sibilant [s], as in English 'sow'; Old Norse initial s is always voiceless, never the English z of 'Susan'.
Short close front unrounded [i], held brief — the vowel of this name is short i, not the long í; Old Norse orthography writes both with one letter.
Intervocalic g is the voiced velar fricative [ɣ] — a softened, gargled gh as in Spanish lago, never a hard stop between vowels.
Short rounded front [ʏ] — the Old Norse y: round the lips while saying i, as in German hübsch or French lune, kept short.
Voiced alveolar nasal [n], clean and final; Old Norse feminine names end in a fully sounded consonant, not a swallowed one.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SEE-ghyn' — two syllables with the weight on the first, the g a soft gargled gh, the y rounded like German ü and kept short; never 'SIGH-in' and never 'sig-WIN'.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Sigyn, wife of Loki; the name is attested only for this goddess, never as a human personal name in the medieval record.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᛋᛁᚴᚢᚾ (sikun), a normalized phonetic reconstruction — the sixteen-rune row distinguishes neither k from g nor short from long vowels.

kin.label: Skaldic verse
kin.form: Sigyn in Þjóðólfr of Hvinir's Haustlöng (c. 900), where Loki is 'farmr Sigynjar arma' — the burden of Sigyn's arms.

kin.label: Modern Scandinavian
kin.form: Sigyn, a rare but living given name in Sweden, revived from the Edda.

pronunciation.note: Sigyn is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The y is a rounded vowel in sound, not in spelling; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Loyalty, Wife of Loki
domains.subtitle: The Wife Who Holds the Bowl
domains.lead: Sigyn is the wife of [[loki|Loki]] and the mother of his human sons — and the most patient figure in the whole Norse corpus. When the Æsir bound Loki beneath the earth for the death of Baldr, and [[skadi|Skaði]] fastened a venom-snake above his face, Sigyn took her place beside him with a basin, catching the poison drop by drop. Only when the basin fills and she turns away to empty it does the venom fall on Loki's face — and then he writhes so hard that the whole earth shakes, and men call it an earthquake.

cards.name: The Venom Basin
cards.desc: The bowl Sigyn holds above Loki's face, catching the snake's drip — the one mercy in the whole binding scene, and it is hers alone.

cards.name: The Falling Drop
cards.desc: When the basin is full she must turn away to empty it; for those moments the venom falls unchecked — the gap in mercy, measured in drops.

cards.name: The Three Stones
cards.desc: The three slabs — under shoulders, loins, and knees — to which Loki was bound with his own son's entrails turned to iron: the fixed point of her vigil.

cards.name: The Earthquake
cards.desc: Loki's writhing when the venom strikes: 'then he writhes so hard that all the earth shakes — those are now called earthquakes.'

symbols.name: The venom basin
symbols.meaning: Loyalty made object — the mercy she holds over him, measured drop by drop

symbols.name: The venom-snake
symbols.meaning: Skaði's sentence, fastened above Loki's face — the fixed threat Sigyn stands between

symbols.name: The iron bonds
symbols.meaning: Nari's entrails turned to iron — the binding her vigil softens but cannot loose

symbols.name: The three stones
symbols.meaning: Loki's anchor in the gorge — shoulders, loins, and knees pinned beneath the earth

symbols.name: The earthquake
symbols.meaning: The world shaking when the bowl is lifted — her brief absence, written in tremors

mythology.lead: Sigyn's dossier is small and strangely old: a naming in Snorri's catalogue of the gods, a kenning from a skald of Harald Fairhair's age, one stanza in the oldest poem of the Edda, and then the scene that made her immortal — the binding of Loki, where she does the only thing left to do and does it forever. The tradition never gives her a word to say. It gives her a bowl.

myths.title: The Wife of Loki
myths.text:
Snorri names her in the survey of the Æsir with his usual economy: Loki's wife is named Sigyn, and their son is Nari or Narfi. That is the whole introduction — no father, no hall, no office. The same catalogue gives Loki his other family: the giantess [[angrboda|Angrboða]], who bore him the wolf [[fenrir|Fenrir]], the World Serpent, and [[hel|Hel]]. Between the monster-brood and the human sons stands Sigyn, the wife within the walls of Ásgarðr.

That she was already Loki's established wife long before the Eddas were written is proven by the skalds: Þjóðólfr of Hvinir, composing Haustlöng around the year 900, calls Loki 'farmr Sigynjar arma' — the burden of Sigyn's arms — a kenning that works only if every listener already knew whose arms held him. The ásynja þulur preserved with Skáldskaparmál keep her in the catalogue of the goddesses by name.

myths.title: The Captive in the Grove of Kettles
myths.text:
The seeress of Völuspá, the oldest and greatest poem of the Codex Regius, sees the punishment before it happens: a captive lying under the grove of kettles, something evil-minded in form like Loki — 'and there sits Sigyn, by no means happy about her husband. Do you understand yet, or what more?'

The stanza is the whole of her eddic portrait, and it is enough: seated, sorrowing, and staying. A generation of readers has noted what the seeress does not say — that Sigyn is anywhere else. In the oldest witness the tradition has, she is already at her post.

myths.title: The Flyting's Aftermath
myths.text:
Lokasenna ends in a prose coda as brutal as anything in the corpus. Loki, who has slandered every god and goddess at Ægir's feast, is caught and bound across three stones with the entrails of his son Nari, while his other son Narfi is turned into a wolf. [[skadi|Skaði]] takes a venomous snake and fastens it above his face, so that the venom drips down.

Then the prose gives Sigyn her scene: she sits there and holds a basin under the dripping venom, and when the basin is full she goes to pour it out — but while she is gone the venom drips into Loki's face, and he writhes so hard that the whole earth shakes. Those, the text says, are called earthquakes. There he lies bound until Ragnarök — and there, the prose implies, she stays.

myths.title: The Binding of Loki
myths.text:
Snorri sets the same scene at the end of the Baldr cycle, with fuller stagecraft. After the death of [[baldr|Baldr]] the Æsir hunt Loki to Franangr's falls, where he hides in the shape of a salmon and is caught in the net he himself invented. His son Váli — not [[odinn|Óðinn]]'s son of the same name — is changed into a wolf and tears apart his brother Nari; with Nari's entrails the gods bind Loki across three stones, and the bonds turn to iron. Skaði fastens the poison-snake above his face.

And Sigyn, his wife, stands beside him and holds a basin under the dripping venom. When the basin is full she carries it out and empties it; meanwhile the venom falls on Loki's face, and then he writhes so hard against the bonds that all the earth shakes — 'those are now called earthquakes.' Snorri's account and the Lokasenna prose swap which son is gutted and which is made a wolf; they do not differ on the wife with the bowl.

lore.syncretism: Sigyn's truest kin are inside the corpus itself. She is the mirror of [[nanna|Nanna]] — the two wives of the Baldr catastrophe, one following her dead husband into the fire, the other staying beside her living one in the pit; devotion answered by death in the one, by endurance without end in the other. Scholarship has been cool toward grander comparisons. Simek and Orchard treat Sigyn strictly within the Loki complex: her attestation is thin, her etymology only probable, and no cult can be reconstructed from a bowl held over a bound god. Lindow reads the scene as the tradition's darkest domestic image — the flyting's bill coming due at the household, not on the battlefield — and notes that the earthquake aetiology made Sigyn's vigil the medieval North's explanation for the trembling earth. What can be said cleanly is that no other figure in the Edda is defined so entirely by a single act of staying.
lore.culturalLegacy: Sigyn's afterlife is the afterlife of one image. The medieval earthquake-theory — the earth shakes when she lifts the bowl — survived for centuries as the North's household explanation of tremors, and every retelling of Loki's punishment, from the Kearys' Victorian 'Heroes of Asgard' onward, keeps the wife and the basin at the centre of the scene: it is the one moment of grace in the flyting's long aftermath, and illustrators have never been able to leave it out. Nineteenth-century romanticism made her the Edda's type of wifely fidelity; twentieth-century scholarship made her the test case for how much a single stanza and a prose coda can hold. The name itself went quietly back into use — Sigyn is a rare but living given name in Sweden — and modern Heathen and Ásatrú communities honour her as the goddess of loyalty, fidelity, and endurance under an unjust sentence: the one who stays.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Sigyn is the Edda's one study of fidelity without hope. Every other loyalty in the corpus has a horizon: vengeance will come, the ransom may succeed, Ragnarök will end it. Hers has none — the binding is until the world's end, the snake does not sleep, the basin fills at the same rate forever. And the tradition is pitilessly exact about the terms of her mercy: it is not that she fails. It is that she must sometimes put the bowl down.

In that gap the whole myth lives. The Norse imagination looked at the shaking earth and did not see a god's rage or a giant's hammer — it saw the moments when a devoted woman turns away to empty a basin. Loki deserves his sentence; the texts never pretend otherwise. Sigyn is not there to acquit him. She is there because love does not consult the verdict, and the oldest poem in the collection already knew it: there sits Sigyn, by no means happy — and there she sits.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as Sigyn — Old Norse, attested 13th c. CE in the Codex Regius and related codices. In the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛋᛁᚴᚢᚾ (sikun), a normalized phonetic reconstruction: the sixteen-rune row distinguishes neither k from g nor short from long vowels, so the runic form underspecifies exactly the features the manuscript spelling records. No runic attestation of the theonym survives. The normalized form is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — which fixes the name in Tier 2. Because it is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: sigyn.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Sigyn has one candidate image and it is famous: the Gosforth Cross in Cumbria, carved in the first half of the tenth century, whose programme of Ragnarök scenes includes a bound male figure with a smaller figure kneeling beside him holding a bowl — standardly interpreted as Loki bound and Sigyn with the basin (Bailey; Lindow), the one Viking-Age monument that may show her at her post. Otherwise she is a wholly textual goddess: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit names her, and no other image can be securely identified. Her attestation hangs on the manuscript witnesses of the Loki cycle — the Codex Regius for Völuspá 35 and the Lokasenna prose epilogue, and the Codex Regius, Codex Wormianus, and Uppsala codices of Snorri's Edda for Gylfaginning 34 and 50 — with Þjóðólfr's Haustlöng (c. 900), quoted in Skáldskaparmál, proving the kenning 'the burden of Sigyn's arms' was already current a century before Iceland's conversion.
